newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Man pleads not guilty to Tasmania massacre.
newsitem.headline: Man pleads not guilty to Tasmania massacre.

text.p: The man accused of the worst mass killing in modern Australian history pleaded not guilty to 35 counts of murder in a Tasmanian court on Monday.
Martin Bryant, 29, also denied 20 charges of attempted murder and 17 lesser charges arising from the massacre on April 28 at the island's historic penal colony of Port Arthur.
Bryant's not-guilty pleas means that the case will have to go to a full trial, expected to start on November 19. Bryant was remanded in custody until the trial.

The Supreme Court of Tasmania in the state capital of Hobart was ringed by heavy security for the hearing, the first time Bryant has appeared in person in court since his arrest the day after the killings.

In a 25-minute hearing, Bryant bent down to a microphone and answered "not guilty" to all 72 charges as they were read in quick succession by the clerk of the court. No basis to his plea was either sought or offered.
Bryant was flanked by three court security officers throughout the hearing.
Dressed in a pale grey suit and with long, curly blond hair falling on to a white, collarless shirt, Bryant showed little emotion as he faced the judge.
He turned only once to face the courtroom where some relatives of the dead sat in a packed public gallery.
"You are a bloody coward, Bryant," shouted Phillip Pears, whose brother Glenn died in the massacre. Ordered out of the court by the judge, Pears added before leaving: "Yours will come soon."
Bryant has been the subject of numerous death threats since his arrest.
On April 28, a sunny Sunday afternoon, a lone gunman walked into the Broad Arrow Cafe at Port Arthur and shot 20 people as they ate their lunch.
Within an hour a further 12 people, including a three-year-old girl, were gunned down either outside the cafe, in their cars, or hiding behind a tree.
Three people, including Glenn Pears, were taken hostage and later found dead in the charred remains of the Seascape guest house near the former penal colony.

The killings led Australia's conservative federal government to institute tough new gun laws under which high-powered and self-loading guns are banned. The law also established a national register of gun owners.

The law still has to be ratified by Australia's six states and two territories, which are responsible for gun laws. Prime Minister John Howard said on Monday he would talk with state leaders in the next few days to work out the details of a costly buy-back scheme for the outlawed weapons.
